Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

mean verb

intend

also intend, mean to, on purpose, I didn’t mean to, what do you mean?, propose to do, I intended to, with the best intentions, mean well, how do you mean?, how so?, do you mean me?, now you know what I mean, I made up my mind not to, I had in mind to

classical

Cic. Fam. 14.11: nōbīs erat in animō Cicerōnem ad Caesarem mittere
Liv. praef. 6: ea nec adfirmāre nec refellere in animō est
Traupman 104: in animō habēre (+ inf.)
Traupman 101
Traupman 103: I made up my mind not to hurry, erat in animō nihil festīnāre
Traupman 333

in animō habēre

mean to, intend (with an infinitive)

Also mihi in animō est, with an infinitive.

Other words

  • volō, velle, voluī — mean to, intend

    verb, irregular · also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 19: Hic respondēre voluit, nōn lacessere.; Ter. Eun. 797: Quid tu tibi vīs?; Traupman 103: what do you mean?, quid tibi vīs? · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short: “to intend, purpose, mean”. “I meant to” is often simply volēbam; Quid tibi vīs?, “What do you mean (by this)? What are you after?”.

  • cōgitō, cōgitāre, cōgitāvī, cōgitātum — intend, plan (with an infinitive)

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cato, Agr. 1.1: praedium quom parāre cōgitābis · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short: “to have something in mind, to intend, meditate, design, plan”.

  • cōnsultō — on purpose

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.27: an cōnsultō et cōgitātā fīat injūria · Wiktionary

    Nōn cōnsultō fēcī: I didn’t mean to.

  • imprūdēns, imprūdentis — without meaning to, unawares

    adjective, third declension · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 880: fēcī imprūdēns quam sciēns; Traupman 104: by mistake, imprūdēns · Declension on Wiktionary

    Agrees with the subject: imprūdēns fēcī, I did it without meaning to.

  • optimō animō — with the best intentions, meaning well

    ablative of quality or manner; Traupman: optimō animō ūtēns · also used · classical · Cic. Phil. 3.2: sunt enim optimō animō, summō cōnsiliō, of the best disposition (Lewis & Short), s.v. bonus; Traupman 101: optimō animō ūtēns; Traupman 333

  • Quī istuc? — how so? how do you mean?

    quī, the old ablative, “how?”, with istuc, “that (of yours)” · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 2.3.10: Quī istuc? Quae rēs tē sollicitat autem? (Lewis & Short s.v. autem); Traupman 103: how do you mean that?, quī istuc vīs?

    Asks how what the other person has just said can be so. Traupman adds vīs; the comic poets ask with the bare Quī istuc?.

  • dēstinō, dēstināre, dēstināvī, dēstinātum — intend, resolve, design

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Traupman 333 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

Examples

  • ea nec adfirmāre nec refellere in animō est

    I don’t mean either to vouch for these stories or to refute them.Liv. praef. 6

  • Hic respondēre voluit, nōn lacessere.

    He meant to answer, not to provoke.Ter. Ph. 19

  • Quid tu tibi vīs?

    What do you mean by it?Ter. Eun. 797

  • Nōn cōnsultō fēcī, tata.

    I didn’t mean to, Daddy.composed

  • Erat mihi in animō rēctā proficīscī domum.

    I intended to set out straight for home.Traupman 101

  • Mēne vīs? — Tē.

    Do you mean me? — Yes, you.Traupman 103

  • Scīs jam quid loquar.

    Now you know what I mean.Traupman 103

See also mean, want, think, really?.
